list.listitem: As part of their cardiovascular risk assessment, patients should be screened for obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes.B

Lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, and weight loss decrease the eventual laboratory diagnosis of diabetes, but not the long-term cardiovascular, neurologic, or renal complications of diabetes.B
Diabetic and weight-loss medications may delay the onset of type 2 diabetes, but the medications may be expensive, have side effects, and are not effective long term.B
Treatment is centered on treating the individual components of the metabolic syndrome (ie, obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and/or type 2 diabetes). C

background.definition: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of conditions including insulin resistance, and/or abdominal obesity, hypertension (HTN), and dyslipidemia that is associated with an increased risk for cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).

list.listitem: 34.2% of the adult US population has metabolic syndrome.
4.8% to 7% of the young adult (18 to 30 years of age) population has metabolic syndrome.
4% to 5% of children have metabolic syndrome.
Non-Hispanic black men are less likely than non-Hispanic white men to have metabolic syndrome (OR 0.77).
Non-Hispanic black women are more likely than non-Hispanic white women to have metabolic syndrome (OR 1.20).

Patients with metabolic syndrome have higher utilization and healthcare costs compared with patients without metabolic syndrome. Average annual costs differed by a factor of 1.6 ($5732 vs $3581) overall and by a factor of 1.3 when stratified by diabetes (diabetes $7896 vs $6038; no diabetes $4476 vs $3422).
Metabolic syndrome is a risk factor for developing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
Metabolic syndrome is associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality (RR 1.23) and cardiovascular disease mortality (RR 1.24).
Metabolic syndrome is highly associated with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in patients under 45 years of age with a prevalence of 51.5% vs 26% of age-matched controls.
Inactive lifestyle
Atherogenic diet
Endothelial dysfunction
Chronic low-grade inflammation
Genetic factors
Abdominal obesity and insulin resistance lead to atherogenic dyslipidemia.
Insulin resistance and hypertension lead to endothelial dysfunction.
Atherogenic dyslipidemia and endothelial dysfunction lead to atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease (CVD).
As part of their cardiovascular risk assessment, patients should be screened for obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes.B
Lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, and weight loss will slow the progression to diabetes, but do not decrease the long-term consequences of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).B

Diabetic medications, obesity medications, and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-Is)/angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) may slow the progression to diabetes. However, side effects are common. It is unclear if progression to T2DM is stopped or delayed, as there is no evidence for improved patient-oriented outcomes.B .
Adults 40 to 70 years of age that are overweight or obese should be screened for T2DM.
Patients 18 years of age and older should be screened regularly for hypertension.
All adults should be screened for obesity.
Adult males 35 years of age and older should be screened for lipid disorders. Men aged 20 to 35 years should be screened for lipid disorders if they are at high risk for coronary heart disease.
Adult women 20 years of age and older should be screened for lipid disorders if they are at increased risk for coronary heart disease.
Clinicians should offer to refer patients with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m2 or higher for an intensive multicomponent behavioral intervention.
Metformin treatment in persons at risk for T2DM reduces new-onset diabetes by 40% over a three-year period (OR 0.6; absolute risk reduction 6%; NNT = 12.5).

Dietary changes, exercise, or a combination of the two decreased the onset of frank diabetes by approximately 50% from a baseline of 37% (HR 0.50). Acarbose, metformin, or glipizide decreased the onset of diabetes by approximately 30% (HR 0.70). Orlistat decreased the likelihood of developing diabetes by approximately the same amount (HR 0.44). The number needed to treat was estimated to be between 5 to 10. The preventative effects of medications were not maintained once they were stopped and it is not clear whether diabetes onset was prevented or just delayed.

Patients at high risk for developing T2DM were less likely to develop T2DM if taking rosiglitazone than if given a placebo (10.6% vs 25% of control patients, NNT = 7). However, 0.5% of patients taking rosiglitazone developed congestive heart failure vs 0.1% of control patients (NNH = 220).

Patients with an impaired fasting glucose were less likely to develop T2DM if they were prescribed acarbose. The rates of side effects were high, however. It is unclear if acarbose prevents or delays the onset of T2DM.
There is no firm evidence that alpha-glucosidase inhibitors have a beneficial effect on cardiovascular mortality or cardiovascular events.

Comprehensive lifestyle changes decrease the eventual laboratory diagnosis of T2DM in high-risk patients, but do not decrease the long-term cardiovascular, neurologic, or renal consequences of T2DM over long-term follow up.
The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin therapy in patients 60 to 69 years of age who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one.

Initiate low-dose aspirin therapy for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 50 to 59 years of age who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk, are not at increased risk of bleeding, have a life expectancy of at least 10 years, and are willing to take low-dose aspirin for at least 10 years.
Gastric bypass surgery, performed by and experienced surgeon, should be offered to patients with severe obesity (BMI of at least 40 kg/m2) or other risk factors for premature death.
Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when patients meet standard criteria based on weight, abdominal circumference, lipids, blood pressure, and blood sugar (see ). C
See for the definitions of metabolic syndrome recommended by various national and international organizations.
To diagnose metabolic syndrome according to the standard criteria in , it is necessary to measure the patient’s waist circumference and blood pressure, and to determine their body mass index.
BMI below 30 kg/m2 has a NPV of 91.1% to rule out metabolic syndrome. (PMID 30817613)
To diagnose metabolic syndrome according to the standard criteria in , it is necessary to measure the patient’s fasting glucose and obtain a lipid panel.
Suspect metabolic syndrome in patients that are overweight or obese and have hypertension.
Confirm the diagnosis using published diagnostic criteria ().
Treatment is focused on addressing each of the components of the diagnoses. See separate chapters for hypertension, T2DM, obesity, and hyperlipidemia for details.
Treatment is centered on treating the individual components of the syndrome (eg, hypertension, obesity, hyperlipidemia, and T2DM). C
Lifestyle modifications such as weight loss, diet, and exercise should be recommended.B

Drug therapy, including medications for T2DM and weight loss, reduces later laboratory diagnosis of diabetes. There is concern for cost, side effects, and loss of effect if these medications are discontinued.B
Please see for an overview of drug therapy.
Gastric bypass surgery, performed by an experienced surgeon, should be considered for patients with marked obesity (BMI of at least 40 kg/m2) and other risk factors for premature death.

A systematic review of 43 studies with over 40 000 patients found that lifestyle modifications significantly reduced the incidence of T2DM (7.4 vs 11.4 cases/100 person-years, p <0.05, NNT = 25). The same systematic review concluded that medications provide a similar benefit (NNT = 25).

Lifestyle changes such as diet and exercise may slow the progression from prediabetes to diabetes, but have not been proven to decrease cardiovascular, neurologic, or renal consequences of T2DM over long-term follow-up.

Weight-loss strategies using dietary, physical activity, or behavioral interventions produced significant improvements in weight and decreased in the incidence of T2DM. However, quality of life and mortality data were not included in the study.
A Mediterranean diet has been advocated based on improvements in metabolic measures from the PREDIMED randomized trial. The overall trial found a reduction in cardiovascular events in all patients.
A randomized trial of time restricted eating (8-10 hour period) found a small reduction in HgbA1C (0.1%) after 3 months.
Blueberries (1 cup/day) improve lipid status but not insulin resistance or blood pressure in metabolic syndrome.
The diagnosis of metabolic syndrome in patients with acute myocardial infarction is common and is associated with worse outcomes.B
Metabolic syndrome is associated with greater severity and chronicity of depression in older adults.B
Metabolic syndrome fluctuates greatly during the transition from adolescence to adulthood.B

Patients with isolated metabolic syndrome (metabolic syndrome without a diagnosis of hypertension or T2DM) are at increased risk for developing hypertension, T2DM, and obesity. They are not at an increased risk of mortality or heart failure.B

In patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI), 69% meet the criteria for metabolic syndrome during AMI hospitalization and 63% meet the criteria at 1 month. Patients meeting the criteria for metabolic syndrome at the time of their AMI but not 1 month later had a lower likelihood of rehospitalization or death over 12 months than those with persistent metabolic syndrome at 1 month (27% vs 37%).B

The presence of metabolic syndrome in older adults with depression is associated with greater severity and chronicity of depression. This may be due to a decreased response to antidepressant medications in this population.
Metabolic syndrome leads to increased motor symptoms in Parkinson’s disease.
Moderate-intensity physical activity reduces the risk of persistent major mobility disability (HR = 0.57) in older persons with metabolic syndrome, but not in those without metabolic syndrome.
Compared with subjects without metabolic syndrome, those with metabolic syndrome have an increased risk of frailty (OR 1.85).

The prevalence of metabolic syndrome increases during the menopausal transition independent of age and other covariates. The odds of developing metabolic syndrome per year in perimenopause are 1.45, and 1.24 after menopause.
During the transition from adolescence to adulthood, metabolic syndrome is highly unstable and fluctuates even among those who have obesity and are gaining weight.
In a randomized crossover study of obese children 9 to 18 years of age, 1 g of metformin given twice daily led to a mean weight loss of 10 pounds at the end of 6 months compared with placebo.

feature.feature_body:

Diagnostic: 1 required criterion and 2 other criteria
TG ≥177 mg/dL or HDL-C <39 mg/dL
BP ≥140/≥90 mmHg or on BP med
Glucose: IGT, IFG but not DM
IDF 2005 Abdominal obesity (population specific) TG ≥150 mg/dL or on TG lowering Rx
Diagnostic: 1 required criterion and 2 other criteria
HDL-C <40 mg/dL in men or <50 mg/dL in women or on HDL improvement Rx
BP ≥130/≥85 mmHg or on BP med
Glucose: ≥100 mg/dL or dx of DM
WHO 1998 Insulin resistance (IGT, IFG, Type 2 DM or reduced insulin sensitivity) Abdominal obesity (waist/hip ratio >0.9 in men; >0.85 in women) or BMI >30 kg/m2
Diagnostic: 1 required criterion and 2 other criteria
TG ≥150 mg/dL or HDL-C <35 mg/dL in men or <39 mg/dL in women
BP ≥140/≥90 mmHg
Glucose: IGT, IFG or Type 2 DM
Microalbuminuria†
IGT = impaired glucose tolerance; two-hour plasma glucose value during a 75 g OGTT between 140 and 199 mg/dL. IFG = impaired fasting glucose; fasting plasma glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL. TG = triglyceride. HDL-C = high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. DM = diabetes mellitus. Rx = pharmacological treatment. BP = blood pressure. †Microalbuminuria defined as urinary albumin excretion of ≥20µg/min or albumin-to-creatinine ratio of ≥30mg/g. AACE: American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists; AHA/NHLBI: American Heart Association and the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute; ATP III: Adult Treatment Panel III; EGIR: European Group for Study of Insulin Resistance; IDF: International Diabetes Foundation; WHO = World Health Organization.

feature.caption: Pharmaceutical interventions for weight loss
feature.feature_body:
Medication Efficacy Adverse Effects
Liraglutide (Saxenda and Victoza) Mean weight loss of 6 kg over 3 years compared with 2 kg in placebo group. Increased risk of thyroid C-cell tumor, more frequent gastrointestinal complaints from delayed gastric emptying
Among those with T2DM, the mean time to diagnosis was 99 weeks in the liraglutide group and 87 weeks in the control group (3-month difference).
Orlistat (Xenical and Alli) Weight loss average of 8.8 kg after 1 year compared with 5.8 kg in placebo group. Rebound weight gain if discontinued
Orlistat plus hypocaloric diet favorably modified several cardiovascular risk factors in patients with both metabolic syndrome and T2DM compared with those on hypocaloric diet alone after 6 months.
Orlistat plus lifestyle interventions reduced the incidence of T2DM by 37% in high-risk patients compared with placebo and lifestyle changes alone.
Metformin In a small crossover RCT of 28 patients in a pediatric endocrine clinic, 1 g of metformin twice daily improved metabolic measures more than placebo. After 6 months, there was a weight loss of 4.4 kg, BMI decrease of 1.3 kg/m2, waist circumference decrease of 2.8 cm, and fasting insulin decrease of 2 mU/L. Risk of lactic acidosis
A meta-analysis of 6 RCTs concluded that metformin dosed at 1000 mg to 1500 mg per day delayed the onset of diabetes over the 3 years of the study with an absolute risk reduction of 6% (CI 4-8). The mean trial duration was 1.8 years (NNT = 13).
Thiazolidinediones (Avandia and Actos) Rosiglitazone: 10.6% of patients taking rosiglitazone developed diabetes compared with 25% in the placebo group (NNT = 7). Risk of heart failure: 12.4% per year in patient receiving a thiazolidinedione compared with 8.6% per year in the placebo group
Phentermine-topiramate Weight loss of 8 kg to 10 kg after one-year period compared with 1.4 kg in the placebo group. Dry mouth, constipation, paresthesia
Phentermine-topiramate was less effective for weight loss in the second year of use, although most individuals were able to maintain the weight they lost in year one.
Sympathomimetic drugs (Phentermine and Diethylpropion) Phentermine: weight loss of 7.2 kg over 12-week period compared with 1.9 kg in the placebo group. Increased heart rate and blood pressure
Diethylpropion: weight loss of 1 kg to 10 kg over 25-week duration compared with the placebo group. Dry mouth, constipation, nervousness
Lorcaserin (Belviq) In a double-blinded RCT of 6818 patients with T2DM who are overweight or obese with BMI>=27kg/m2, 16.3% of locaserin-treated patients vs. 13.7% of placebo-treated patients experienced remission. Among 3991 patients with prediabetes, 8.5% of lorcaserin-treated patients vs. 10.3% of placebo-treated patients developed T2DM (NNT=56). Among 1193 patients without overt T2DM, 6.7% of lorcaserin-treated patients vs. 8.5% of placebo-treated patients developed T2DM (NNT=58). Lorcaserin-treated patients were less likely to develop persistent microalbuminuria (7.8%) compared to placebo-treated patients (10.0%). Hypoglycemia occured more frequently in lorcaserin-treated patients (0.4%) compare to placebo-treated patients (0.1%).
In a double-blinded RCT with total of 12,000 patients with BMI >=27 kg/m2 who had heart disease or CVD risk factors received loracaserin 10 mg twice Daily or placebo. More patients in the Lorcaserin-treated group lost at least 10% of their body weight compared to placebo group (14.6% vs 4.8%; P<0.001; NNT = 10) over 3.3-year follow-up period. dizziness, fatigue, headache
Note: The NIH guidelines on obesity recommend considering pharmaceutical therapy for weight loss in patients with a BMI of ≥30 kg/m2 or ≥27 kg/m2 in the presence of comorbidities related to excess adiposity.
